title: PrivateNet handoff: DNS, SNI, quant & batching primer
summary: Introductory deep dive on Citadel Labs' PrivateNet handoff planning. Focus areas: PrivateLink setup, split-horizon DNS for service discovery, SNI-based routing for shared endpoints, NAT/egress considerations (hairpinning, multi-subnet), KV cache behavior and sticky-session expectations, continuous batching tradeoffs, and expected quantization impacts on latency. Action items: run baseline latency tests, share security & deployment checklist, schedule a pilot weekend for end-to-end connectivity tests.

INT8/FP16 quantization effects on tail latency

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-01-19
Start: 15:02 UTC
Duration: ~90 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Eric (Redwood SE), Rafiq (Citadel Platform), Lina (Citadel SRE), Sanjay (Citadel CTO)
---
Summary (auto): walkthrough of private VPC handoff with emphasis on DNS, NAT, SNI routing, KV cache and quant tradeoffs. Agreed on pilot weekend and a list of artifacts to exchange.
---
[00:00:00] Maya: All right, thanks everyone for joining, we'll kick off. quick intro, i'm Maya, i'll run the logistics side, Eric will go deep on runtime and networking.
[00:00:08] Eric: Hey folks, hi, uh, thanks for the time. So the plan today is to map your PrivateNet topology to Redwood's Private deployment constraints and call out common gotchas — split-horizon DNS, SNI routing when you front with internal ALBs, and how KV cache and batching interact with NAT and sticky sessions.
[00:00:25] Sanjay: Sounds good. high level — we're moving from a hosted pilot to a private VPC sac setup, want predictable p99 and secure connectivity. We care about: encrypted egress, no public IPs on compute, and audit logs.
[00:00:40] Maya: noted. quick qualification: are you planning cross-account PrivateLink or VPC peering?
[00:00:46] Rafiq: PrivateLink cross-account, we want the product plane in our account, and Redwood's PrivateLink endpoint in a shared services VPC, then NACLs and route tables to our worker subnets.
[00:00:56] Eric: cool — PrivateLink fits nicely but split-horizon DNS is the usual sticking point. If your resolver returns the private privatelink DNS name inside the VPC, great. If not, you'll see egress out to public endpoints and weird TLS SNI mismatches.
[00:01:14] Lina: Can you expand on SNI mismatches? We use an NLB that terminates TLS, then routes by SNI to different model variants.
[00:01:20] Eric: Sure. So Redwood exposes endpoints that expect SNI to carry the model route (example: model-a.app.redwood.internal). If your NLB or custom proxy rewrites or strips SNI, the runtime may route to the wrong model variant or fall back, which increases latency. Also if you front with a TLS terminator that re-encrypts downstream without preserving the original SNI, you'll lose routing fidelity.
[00:01:44] Speaker 1 (Rafiq?): yeah, so we do TLS terminate at the edge and re-encrypt. we can preserve SNI in the re-encryption stage but some of our older proxies don't.
[00:01:53] Eric: Right, that's a common ops caveat. For the pilot, try to preserve the client SNI all the way to the Redwood PrivateLink endpoint or do layer 4 passthrough at the edge for the inference path.
[00:02:05] [00:02:05] Lina: quick Q on DNS: we use split-horizon via Route53 inbound endpoints, resolvers in a dedicated resolver subnet. Will Redwood's runtime call back to our resolver for model downloads or only for control plane?
[00:02:19] Maya: We can work both ways. Model artifacts are typically pulled by the private plane, but runtime will do health checks and service discovery that can use your DNS. The main ask is to keep the private names resolvable inside the VPC so the traffic doesn't hairpin to the public internet.
[00:02:34] Eric: Also watch resolver TTLs. Short TTLs plus aggressive KV cache eviction can cause lots of extra lookups; that shows up as CPU on sidecars and increases p95.
[00:02:44] Rafiq: we're planning 30s TTLs for dev and 300s for prod. is 300s ok?
[00:02:50] Eric: 300s is fine, fewer flapping lookups. For the KV cache, the bigger concern is key cardinality and eviction policy — if you have many unique request prefixes (chat sessions), the cache hit-rate goes low and the runtime spends more time in KV miss logic.
[00:03:06] Lina: can you recommend cache sizing? we expect 25k concurrent chat sessions in peak.
[00:03:12] Eric: Rough rule: KV entries per session depend on session length and model tokenization. For 25k sessions, start with a cache heap large enough for ~200k keys (so approx 8–10 entries per session), monitor miss-rate, and scale upward. We'll give you sample config. Also enable sticky routing for long-lived sessions so requests for the same conversation hit the same worker and reuse local KV.
[00:03:36] [00:03:36] Sanjay: sticky routing — we worry about even distribution and overload. if we pin too many sessions to a single instance, isn't that a hot spot?
[00:03:43] Eric: It can be. Redwood's runtime supports session affinity with bounded eviction: we use consistent hashing with a lease TTL so that long idle sessions eventually reassign. Combine that with autoscaling policies tuned to session CPU; that avoids permanent hot spots.
[00:03:59] Maya: quick interjection — from a product POV, we also offer KV prefix caching (shared prefixes across sessions) which improves hit rate for instruction-heavy prompts.
[00:04:09] Lina: neat. moving to egress: hairpinning — we've had issues where internal traffic to privatelink endpoints went out through a NAT gateway and back, adding ~60–80ms. how do we avoid that?
[00:04:21] Eric: That sounds like resolver returning public IPs or route table misconfig. PrivateLink interfaces must be in the same AZ subnets or have correct VPC endpoints; also ensure source/dest checks and route tables prefer local endpoints. Another pattern: use an egress-only proxy per AZ that can keep path local and preserve source IPs.
[00:04:39] Rafiq: We also use multiple subnets per AZ for isolation. Any MTU considerations? we've seen truncation when gzip + TLS + large payloads happen.
[00:04:47] Eric: MTU matters, especially if you put IPsec between sites; 1500 is typical, but if you tunnel, reduce to 1400 and test. For inference payloads, try to keep the token chunk sizes under your path MTU, and enable path MTU discovery on your proxies.
[00:05:02] [00:05:02] Lina: ok good. now batching — the big question: continuous batching lowers per-token cost, but increases latency. We're targeting sub-120ms p50 and p99 under 400ms for simple prompts. thoughts?
[00:05:15] Eric: Continuous batching has a parameter you tune: max batch delay (ms) and max batch size. For sub-120ms p50, set max batch delay to 10–15ms and a moderate max batch size (e.g., 32). That gives throughput without blowing p50. For p99 under 400ms, you also need fast KV cache hits and sticky sessions so many requests are single-token cache hits and bypass heavy compute.
[00:05:40] Maya: also quantization influences that — INT8 can reduce compute time per token but may slightly increase CPU for dequant/quant steps and change tail characteristics. Eric, any numbers?
[00:05:50] Eric: In our labs, INT8 reduced median token latency by ~25% on T4-style hardware but p99 sometimes improved only 10–12% because of dequant jitter and memory fragmentation. Also watch for generation noise: sometimes INT8 requires small prompt engineering tweaks. FP16 is less risky but less compression. We'll supply benchmark sheets.
[00:06:10] Rafiq: Are there runtime fallbacks? if INT8 falls through or regresses, can we auto-fail to FP16?
[00:06:17] Eric: Yes, we support dynamic model variants and automatic fallback based on quality/regression alerts. You can pin a percent of traffic to INT8 for canarying. For private deployments, that requires model artifacts for both variants in your artifact store or accessible to the private plane.
[00:06:33] [00:06:33] Sanjay: Regarding observability: we'd like per-route token breakdown and KV hit-rate dashboards. what telemetry can you surface?
[00:06:42] Maya: Redwood Console in Private mode can push metrics to your Prometheus, and we can also export traces to your tracing backend. For private deployments we set up agent collectors that ship only metrics (no payloads) if you want strict data residency.
[00:06:56] Lina: ok that's important. one more on certs — we use customer-managed certs via ACM. How do we rotate TLS certs for the PrivateLink endpoint?
[00:07:05] Eric: For PrivateLink we recommend using your ACM cert on the NLB that fronts the endpoint. Rotation is typically a blue/green swap: provision new cert, add to NLB listeners, then drain old cert. We'll provide runbook steps.
[00:07:18] [00:07:18] Rafiq: let's talk pilot weekend logistics — we want to run an e2e test with 2 AZs, 4 worker subnets, and simulate 5k concurrent sessions. Redwood suggested a controlled load test.
[00:07:29] Eric: We'll provide a perf harness and a script that ramps to 5k chats with a mix of short prompts and longer streaming generations. Important: for realistic KV load, simulate multi-turn chat with session IDs so KV hotness patterns emerge.
[00:07:44] Maya: action item recap: we'll send the checklist, you'll provision the subnets, Eric will give KV + batching configs, Rafiq will run baseline tests and share logs.
[00:07:55] Sanjay: timeline wise, aim to get pilot by the last weekend of January.
[00:07:59] Maya: sounds good. any final questions?
[00:08:02] Lina: small note — our security team will ask for SOC2 artifact and any KMS integration docs.
[00:08:08] Maya: we'll share SOC2 and the KMS guide as part of the pack.
[00:08:12] [00:08:12] Eric: Ok one last tip: if you see p99 jumps that correlate with DNS rotation windows, raise your resolver TTLs and keep KV cache warm during rollout windows.
[00:08:24] Rafiq: great, thanks everyone.
[00:08:27] Maya: thanks all, we'll follow up with the artifacts and set up the pilot weekend invite.
